ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

#| echo: false

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = 0.304", "p = 0.157"), Sentence = c("In contrast, no significant difference in motor improvement following DBS was observed between subgroups (p = 0.304), indicating that T1-WMHypoV burden is associated with pharmacological responsiveness but does not predict DBS-related benefit. reuse, remix, or adapt this material for any purpose without crediting the original authors. this preprint (which was not certified by peer review) in the Public Domain.", "In NMOSD, stratification using the high-deviation threshold (centile > 0.95) did not reveal a significant difference in disability progression between subgroups (p = 0.157)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 439 columns across 12 data files.
#### Issues Identified

8 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("Datasets/Dataset-diseases/MR_measures.xlsx [aseg.vol.table]", "Datasets/Dataset-diseases/MR_measures.xlsx [aseg.vol.table]", "Datasets/Dataset-individual/MR_measures.xlsx [aseg.vol.table]", "Datasets/Dataset-individual/MR_measures.xlsx [aseg.vol.table]", "Datasets/Dataset-new/MR_measures.xlsx [aseg.vol.table]", "Datasets/Dataset-new/MR_measures.xlsx [aseg.vol.table]", "Datasets/Dataset-norms/MR_measures.xlsx [aseg.vol.table]", "Datasets/Dataset-norms/MR_measures.xlsx [aseg.vol.table]" ), Column = c("Left.Inf.Lat.Vent", "Right.Inf.Lat.Vent", "Left.Inf.Lat.Vent", "Right.Inf.Lat.Vent", "Left.Inf.Lat.Vent", "Right.Inf.Lat.Vent", "Left.Inf.Lat.Vent", "Right.Inf.Lat.Vent"), Issues = c("🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: lat)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: lat)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: lat)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: lat)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: lat)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: lat)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: lat)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: lat)" )), row.names = c(NA, -8L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 12 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: White matter hypointensity on T1-weighted MRI (T1-WMHypo), a putative marker of white matter pathophysiological changes, has been less systematically investigated than the widely studied T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (T2-FLAIR) hyperintensity lesions.
Here, we built the lifespan normative reference and assessed the clinical significance of T1-WMHypo across various brain disorders using a large multicenter dataset.

White matter (WM) abnormalities are a hallmark of brain aging and a wide spectrum of neurological disorders (1, 2).

text.text: Among the available imaging markers, white matter hyperintensity (WMHyper) detected on T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (T2-FLAIR) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been extensively investigated and is widely regarded as a core imaging marker of white matter injury (3).
text.formatted: Among the available imaging markers, white matter hyperintensity (WMHyper) detected on T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (T2-FLAIR) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been extensively investigated and is widely regarded as a core imaging marker of white matter injury <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: T2-FLAIR WMHyper (T2-WMHyper) burden has been consistently associated with cognitive decline, functional impairment, and disease progression across both vascular and neurodegenerative conditions(4, 5), shaping prevailing paradigms of WM pathology (6).
text.formatted: T2-FLAIR WMHyper (T2-WMHyper) burden has been consistently associated with cognitive decline, functional impairment, and disease progression across both vascular and neurodegenerative conditions(4, 5), shaping prevailing paradigms of WM pathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref>.

text.text: However, routine clinical MRI frequently reveals additional signal alterations within WM on T1-weighted imaging (T1WI) that have received far less systematic attention.
This predominant focus on T2-FLAIR-defined WM abnormalities has led to a relative neglect of other WM signal alterations that are frequently observed on routine clinical MRI.
One such feature is WM hypointensity observed on T1WI (T1-WMHypo), characterized by reduced signal intensity relative to surrounding normal-appearing WM.

Previous histopathological and imaging studies have associated T1-WMHypo with heterogeneous tissue alterations, including immature WM fiber, enlarged perivascular space, severe myelin and axonal loss, cystic change or cavitation, fibrosis, mineral deposition (e.g., calcium or iron), glymphatic system abnormalities (7) (8) (9) (10).
text.formatted: Previous histopathological and imaging studies have associated T1-WMHypo with heterogeneous tissue alterations, including immature WM fiber, enlarged perivascular space, severe myelin and axonal loss, cystic change or cavitation, fibrosis, mineral deposition (e.g., calcium or iron), glymphatic system abnormalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(9)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(10)</ref>.

text.text: Although T1-WMHypo and T2-WMHyper have often been implicitly regarded as reflecting the same underlying pathology such as WM demyelination, a few evidence indicated that these imaging features are not invariably interchangeable, as they showed distinct evolutions (increased T2-WMHyper while decreased T1-WMHypo) during the dementia progression (11) and some T2-WMHyper lesions didn't show T1-hypointense in aging population (12).

text.text: T1 WMHypo and T2 WMHyper may share both spatial and biological overlap, however, they frequently represent different stages or pathophysiological mechanisms of WM alteration (12) (13) (14).

text.text: Despite this potential significance, T1-WMHypo has received substantially less systematic investigation compared with T2-WMHyper detected on T2-FLAIR.
As with other structural brain measures, T1-WMHypo exhibits marked age-dependent variability across the lifespan, accompanied by substantial interindividual heterogeneity at any given age.
Such variability complicates the interpretation of raw T1-WMHypo burden at the individual level and limits its clinical utility in the absence of appropriate reference standards.

In this context, normative modeling has emerged as a robust framework for constructing lifespan reference curves that capture population-level variation and generate individualized deviation scores, an approach already widely applied to other brain structural metrics, including gray matter volume (GMV) and T2-WMHyper volume (T2-WMHyperV) (19) (20) (21) (22) (23).
text.formatted: In this context, normative modeling has emerged as a robust framework for constructing lifespan reference curves that capture population-level variation and generate individualized deviation scores, an approach already widely applied to other brain structural metrics, including gray matter volume (GMV) and T2-WMHyper volume (T2-WMHyperV) <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(19)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(20)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(21)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(23)</ref>.

text.text: Establishing age-and sex-specific normative references for T1-WMHypo is therefore essential for contextualizing individual measurements, improving clinical interpretability, and identifying individuals with an elevated burden who may be at increased clinical risk.

In this study, leveraging a large multicenter dataset of three-dimensional T1-weighted MRI scans from 34,148 healthy volunteers, we established age-and sex-specific normative references for T1-WMHypo volume (T1-WMHypoV).

We then quantified individual deviation patterns across 21 neurological and psychiatric disorders (7,587 patients) and examined the correlation between T1-WMHypoV deviations and other brain structural metrics, the value of T1-WMHypoV deviations in disease classification, clinical correlation, treatment response, and disease progression.

text.text: Further, we compared the relationship and clinical relevance between T1-WMHyo and T2-WMHyper, as well as spatial-temporal analyses of T1-WMHypo across healthy controls (HCs) and brain disorders.

Univariate analyses and partial correlations additionally adjusted for T2-WMHyperV yielded largely consistent correlations, with attenuated effect sizes (r values) after accounting for conventional T2-WMHyper burden.

text.text: The spatial T1-WMHypo distribution showed a consistent temporal (along the age axis) pattern with the development and aging patterns of whole brain T1-WMHypoV.

Specifically, the T1-WMHypo distribution involved the periventricular regions as well as gray-white matter junction especially in children aged 4-10 years, and then the distribution of gray-white matter junction disappeared, and was mainly located around periventricular regions during the younger and middle life, and then started to expand from the periventricular regions to deep WM with the aging process.

The development and aging trajectories of these regional T1-WMHypoV were consistent with those of whole brain T1-WMHypoV, showing J-shaped trajectories, reaching the lowest burden around 25 (median, 24.84 and range, 21.77-28.40) years.
In addition, disorder-specific spatial deviations of T1-WMHypoV were observed, indicating the different brain regional involvements across disorders.

These regional T1-WMHypoV normative references and their derived deviations provided additional information for the interpretation of pathophysiology in normal development and aging, and pathology across both neurological and psychiatric disorders.

This study established age-and sex-specific normative references for T1-WMHypoV across the human lifespan using a large international multicenter dataset and revealed its potential in both neurological and psychiatric disorders.
(1) The derived lifespan trajectory follows a non-linear J-shaped pattern, with a modest decline from childhood to young adulthood and a progressive age-related increase beginning in midlife.
(2) Using these normative references, patients across various disorders showed significantly greater T1-WMHypo burden than age-and sex-matched HCs.

T1-WMHypo deviations could contribute to differential diagnosis, and elevated T1-WMHypo burden was consistently associated with brain atrophy, cognitive impairment, treatment response in PD, and disease progression in MS and NMOSD. previously reported normative patterns of T2-FLAIR defined WMHyper in adult populations from both Western and Chinese cohorts (20, 21).
text.formatted: T1-WMHypo deviations could contribute to differential diagnosis, and elevated T1-WMHypo burden was consistently associated with brain atrophy, cognitive impairment, treatment response in PD, and disease progression in MS and NMOSD. previously reported normative patterns of T2-FLAIR defined WMHyper in adult populations from both Western and Chinese cohorts <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">21)</ref>.

text.text: While these prior studies focused primarily on adulthood and reported progressive age-related increases in T2-WMHyper burden, our findings extend this perspective by characterizing T1-WMHypo across a much broader age range spanning early childhood to late adulthood, suggesting that both imaging markers may reflect partially overlapping biological processes related to cumulative WM injury during aging.
Importantly, our results further revealed a decline in T1-WMHypo burden during childhood and adolescence, a phase rarely examined in previous studies of T1-WMHypo(30).

This early-life decrease aligns with pediatric neuroimaging literature describing dynamic WM signal changes driven by ongoing myelination and tissue maturation, as well as enlarged perivascular space, indicating that similar T1WI signal alterations may arise from distinct biological substrates at different life stages (18, (31) (32) (33) (34).
text.formatted: This early-life decrease aligns with pediatric neuroimaging literature describing dynamic WM signal changes driven by ongoing myelination and tissue maturation, as well as enlarged perivascular space, indicating that similar T1WI signal alterations may arise from distinct biological substrates at different life stages <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(31)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(32)</ref> <ref type="bibr">(33)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(34)</ref>.

text.text: T1-WMHypoV showed an inverse lifespan trajectory relative to total WMV and a concordant pattern with CSF volume in later life, linking increased T1-WMHypo burden to WM loss and ventricular expansion during brain aging (23).
text.formatted: T1-WMHypoV showed an inverse lifespan trajectory relative to total WMV and a concordant pattern with CSF volume in later life, linking increased T1-WMHypo burden to WM loss and ventricular expansion during brain aging <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(23)</ref>.

text.text: Applying the normative framework across a wide range of neurological and psychiatric disorders revealed substantial heterogeneity in T1-WMHypo deviations.
Across different brain disorders, the magnitude of deviation followed a severity continuum, with the largest effects observed in iNPH and NIID.

These disorders are characterized by diffuse periventricular involvement, cerebrospinal fluid dysregulation, and progressive tissue rarefaction, consistent with extensive WM damage detectable on T1WIs (35, 36).
text.formatted: These disorders are characterized by diffuse periventricular involvement, cerebrospinal fluid dysregulation, and progressive tissue rarefaction, consistent with extensive WM damage detectable on T1WIs <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">36)</ref>.

text.text: High T1-WMHypo burden was also observed in conditions associated with diffuse WM injury and cerebral vascular pathology (e.g., enlarged perivascular space), including MS and CSVD.

In MS, pronounced T1-WMHypo deviations also align with severe tissue injury beyond classical persistent "T1 black holes", including chronic demyelination, axonal loss, matrix destruction, and gliosis, pathological features that contribute to reduced T1 signal intensity and reflect destructive lesion evolution and chronic WM damage (37) (38) (39).
text.formatted: In MS, pronounced T1-WMHypo deviations also align with severe tissue injury beyond classical persistent "T1 black holes", including chronic demyelination, axonal loss, matrix destruction, and gliosis, pathological features that contribute to reduced T1 signal intensity and reflect destructive lesion evolution and chronic WM damage <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(37)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(38)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(39)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, NMOSD and MOGAD did not exhibit significant whole-brain T1-WMHypo deviations despite prominent lesion burden on T2-FLAIR imaging.

This dissociation suggests that T1-WMHypo in such diseases may preferentially reflects more severe axonal damage and may aid in distinguishing inflammatory demyelinating disorders with different degrees of WM damage (40, 41).
text.formatted: This dissociation suggests that T1-WMHypo in such diseases may preferentially reflects more severe axonal damage and may aid in distinguishing inflammatory demyelinating disorders with different degrees of WM damage <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">41)</ref>.

text.text: Moderate but consistent increases in T1-WMHypo burden were observed in neurodegenerative and systemic autoimmune conditions, including AD(42), PSP(43), and SLE(44), likely reflecting secondary WM degeneration accompanying cortical degeneration or systemic inflammatory processes.

Modest yet statistically significant deviations were detected in MCI(45), PD(46), MSA-P(47), epilepsy(48), and MDD(49), i.e., in conditions where WM pathology is generally not considered the primary disease substrate.
Collectively, these findings demonstrate that T1-WMHypo captures a shared yet selectively expressed dimension of underlying WM pathology across brain disorders.

text.text: Across various neurological disorders, higher T1-WMHypo burden was associated with reduced GMV, cortical thinning, subcortical and infratentorial involvement, and cerebrospinal fluid expansion, a pattern characteristic of widespread neurodegenerative processes rather than isolated WM pathology (50) (51) (52) (53).

text.text: In healthy individuals, these structural associations exhibited a clear age-dependent shift, with T1-WMHypo relating predominantly to WMV in younger adults and showing stronger coupling with CSF expansion and cortical thinning in later life.

This transition suggests that T1-WMHypo evolves from a tissue-related feature in early adulthood to an atrophy-associated marker during aging, paralleling trajectories observed in neurodegenerative conditions (54).

text.text: Importantly, many associations persisted after adjustment for T2-WMHyper burden, indicating that T1-WMHypo captures structural alterations not fully accounted for by conventional T2-FLAIR lesion load.

Together, these correlation patterns support the interpretation that T1-WMHypo reflects a convergent process linking WM pathophysiology with GM degeneration and may provide complementary information for characterizing brain aging and disease-related atrophy.

T1-WMHypo had an additional contribution to a majority of disease differential diagnoses beyond multiple brain structural metrics and demographics, highlighting the benefit of including T1-WMHypo in clinical decision making, particularly if T2-FLAIR weighted imaging is unavailable.

Meanwhile, it had consistent associations with clinical functional measures across various neurological disorders, particularly measures of global cognition and information processing speed, in disorders along the cognitive impairment spectrum, including MCI(45) and AD(55).
Similar cognitive associations were also observed in other neurological conditions with recognized cognitive involvement, such as CSVD(56), MSA-C(57), and iNPH (58).

text.text: Importantly, the association between cognitive impairment and T1-WMHypo remains after adjustment for T2-WMHyper burden, indicating that T1-WMHypo captures functional impairment independent of conventional T2-FLAIR lesion burden.

In neuroinflammatory disorders, these associations were predominantly involved in processing speed-related measures, consistent with the established sensitivity of information processing efficiency to widespread WM disruption in demyelinating diseases (60).
text.formatted: In neuroinflammatory disorders, these associations were predominantly involved in processing speed-related measures, consistent with the established sensitivity of information processing efficiency to widespread WM disruption in demyelinating diseases <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(60)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, motor-or mood-related measures showed limited associations with T1-WMHypoV across disorders, indicating relative domain specificity for cognitive function.

Although previous studies have reported links between T1-WMHypo and age-related cognitive decline(61), the use of normative-based centile scores may attenuate cross-sectional brain-behavior correlations by accounting for age-related variance, thereby reducing associations driven by normal aging.
Our findings further indicate that T1-WMHypo burden carries prognostic relevance in various neurological disorders.

Stratification based on T1-WMHypoV deviations showed that individuals with higher hypointensity burden experienced less favorable clinical outcomes, supporting its potential value for disease-specific risk stratification.

In PD, patients with elevated T1-WMHypo burden exhibited more severe motor impairment and derived less benefit from pharmacological treatment, while showing limited additional improvement following DBS.
These findings suggest that T1-WMHypo may constrain the functional reserve of motor networks, thereby modulating therapeutic responsiveness beyond primary dopaminergic deficits (62).
text.formatted: These findings suggest that T1-WMHypo may constrain the functional reserve of motor networks, thereby modulating therapeutic responsiveness beyond primary dopaminergic deficits <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(62)</ref>.

text.text: In demyelinating disorders, T1-WMHypo burden was associated with disease progression.

In MS, higher T1-WMHypo burden was linked to accelerated disability worsening and an increased risk of transition to secondary progressive disease, even after accounting for demographic factors and other brain structural metrics.
This observation is consistent with the interpretation that T1-WMHypo reflects cumulative severe tissue disruption that may contribute to long-term neurological decline(63, 64).
Additional longitudinal MRI analyses further showed progressive increases in T1-WMHypoV in MS and NMOSD, underscoring the disease-specific relevance of this marker.

To clarify the relationships between T1-WMHypoV and T2-WMHyperV, we investigated the correlation between T1-WMHypoV and T2-WMHyperV: they showed consistent patterns in aging but may result from different physiological changes during brain development and aging, and play distinct roles across the lifespan (65).
text.formatted: To clarify the relationships between T1-WMHypoV and T2-WMHyperV, we investigated the correlation between T1-WMHypoV and T2-WMHyperV: they showed consistent patterns in aging but may result from different physiological changes during brain development and aging, and play distinct roles across the lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(65)</ref>.

text.text: The complementary clinical role of T1-WMHypo could be further supported by the clinical association in cases with low T2-WMHyper burdens, implying a partially independent role of T1-WMHypo in addition to T2-WMHyper in disease pathology.
Spatial-temporal findings further displayed the spatial characteristic along the lifespan trajectory and brain disorders, supporting the main findings of whole brain T1-WMHypoV.

They also revealed disease-specific T1-WMHypo spatial distribution, which indicated the disease-specific spatial involvement in brain disorders (22), while their underlying biological mechanisms should be further investigated.
text.formatted: They also revealed disease-specific T1-WMHypo spatial distribution, which indicated the disease-specific spatial involvement in brain disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(22)</ref>, while their underlying biological mechanisms should be further investigated.

text.text: Several limitations should be acknowledged.
First, although the normative reference framework was derived from a large multicenter cohort, most analyses were cross-sectional.
This design limits causal inference and constrains precise estimation of within-subject rates of T1-WMHypo progression.
Future studies with denser longitudinal sampling will be essential to characterize individual trajectories and to validate the temporal sensitivity of T1-WMHypoV as a marker of disease evolution.
Second, T1-WMHypoV was quantified using intensity-based segmentation of three-dimensional T1WIs.
While this approach enables scalable and robust analysis across large datasets, T1-WMHypo reflects a heterogeneous mixture of pathological substrates.
The absence of direct histopathological validation and limited multimodal integration preclude precise attribution of underlying biological mechanisms.

text.text: Integrating multimodal MRI and pathological correlation will be important for disentangling these components.
Third, the present analyses primarily focused on global T1-WMHypo burden.
Although additional regional and spatial analyses were performed, finer-grained compartmental modeling of WM may yield additional disease-specific insights and improve interpretability.
Finally, the prognostic associations observed in only limited brain disorders, while encouraging, require external validation and prospective confirmation before clinical translation.

In summary, this study established age-and sex-specific normative references for T1-WMHypoV across the lifespan and demonstrated their applicability across a wide range of neurological and psychiatric disorders.

By contextualizing individual T1-WMHypo burden within a normative framework, we show that this marker captures a dimension of WM pathophysiological changes partially independent of conventional T2-FLAIR hyperintensity.

Normative deviation patterns vary substantially across diseases, contribute to disease diagnosis and relate to brain structural alterations, functional impairment, and clinical outcomes in various brain disorders.

These findings highlight T1-WMHypoV deviations as an individualized imaging marker for characterizing WM pathophysiological characteristics and advancing precision approaches to brain development, aging and diseases.

text.text: Age or date of birth was extracted from DICOM metadata or obtained directly from participants or their legal guardians.
Available clinical variables included age, sex, and years of education (n=6,442).
Cognitive assessments included MoCA (n=5,636) and MMSE (n=4,850).
Additional cognitive measures were available in subsets of MS, NMOSD and MOGAD patients, including SDMT (n=950) and PASAT (n=926).
Motor and disability assessments were available for specific patient groups.
Among PD patients, UPDRS-III assessments were obtained in the off-medication state (n=788), on-medication state (n=783), and after DBS (n=498).
Baseline and follow-up EDSS scores were available for 850 MS and 394 NMOSD patients, respectively, for neuroinflammatory diseases.
Mood assessment, including Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA, n=1,866) and Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD, n=1,873) were assessed for specific patient groups.
Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (POSI, n=253) for a subset was also acquired.
MRI data were obtained from 146 sites.
All participants underwent three-dimensional T1WIs, typically using a magnetization-prepared rapid gradient echo sequence, with isotropic voxel sizes of 1 mm or less.
A subset of participants additionally underwent T2-weighted FLAIR imaging.
All images were independently reviewed for quality by two trained raters, with discrepancies resolved by consensus involving a third reviewer.
T1WI data were processed using the FreeSurfer (version 7.3.2).
Standard preprocessing steps included correction for intensity non-uniformity, skull stripping, intensity normalization, and registration to Talairach space.

Volumetric measures were extracted from the aseg.stats and aparc.stats outputs, including WMV, cortical GMV, sGMV, cerebellar volume, brainstem volume, CSF volume, mean cortical thickness, total cortical surface area, and TIV.
T1-WMHypoV was derived from intensity-based segmentation within the WM mask as implemented in FreeSurfer.
All T1-WMHypo segmented images were spatially resampled and aligned to a standard template before regional analysis.
WMH were parcellated into seven anatomical regions using the Hammers atlas: corpus callosum, basal ganglia, frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital and insula.
For participants with available T2-weighted FLAIR images, T2-WMHyper segmentation was performed using a previously validated deep learning model (66).
text.formatted: For participants with available T2-weighted FLAIR images, T2-WMHyper segmentation was performed using a previously validated deep learning model <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(66)</ref>.

text.text: Quality control was conducted at multiple stages of the processing pipeline.
Raw MRI scans were visually inspected for motion artifacts and acquisition-related abnormalities.
Automated outlier detection was applied to segmentation outputs, and manual inspection was performed when necessary.
To mitigate residual site-related variability, values exceeding three standard deviations from the site-specific mean were excluded from subsequent analyses.
Normative lifespan models for T1-WMHypoV and other brain structure metrics were constructed using the HC cohort within the GAMLSS implemented in R (version 4.3).
Age and sex were included as fixed effects, and scanning site/center was modeled as a random effect.
A generalized gamma distribution was selected to account for the right-skewed distribution of volume measures.
Age-related effects were modeled using fractional polynomials, with model complexity determined by the Bayesian Information Criterion.
To reduce potential bias in deviation estimation, 10-fold cross-validation was applied.
Individualized centile scores were derived for each participant based on the normative models.
All patient scans were acquired at sites represented in the normative dataset, allowing appropriate adjustment for site-related effects.
Age-related rates of change were estimated by computing the first derivative of the fitted median trajectory across the lifespan.
All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.3, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).
Categorical variables are presented as counts (percentages) and were compared using Pearson's chi-square tests.

Continuous variables are reported as means ± standard deviation and compared using one-way analysis of variance when approximately normally distributed, or as medians with interquartile ranges (or ranges) and compared using the Kruskal-Wallis test when distributions were non-normal.
Normative deviation scores of T1-WMHypoV and other structure metrics were calculated for all participants based on the age-and sex-specific normative reference models.
Group-level differences in deviations T1-WMHypoV and other brain structure metrics between patients and HCs were assessed using Monte Carlo permutation tests with the Welch t statistic.
When available, HCs were matched to patients by age, sex, and scanning site; otherwise, unmatched HCs were used.
Effect sizes were quantified using Cohen's d with 95%CIs.
Multiple comparisons across disease groups were controlled using the FDR procedure.

Significant T1-WMHypoV deviations were observed in the majority of neurological disorders (11/17, 65%) and only major depressive disorder (MDD) in psychiatric disorders (1/4, 25%), with marked heterogeneity in effect magnitude.

Large deviations (|d| ≥ 0.8) were detected in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH, Cohen's d = -2.25, 95%CI [-2.62, -1.88], pFDR < 0.001), neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease (NIID, d = -1.65 [-2.13, -1.17], pFDR < 0.001), cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD, d = -1.26 [-1.37, -1.15], pFDR < 0.001), and MS (d = -0.85 [-1.09, -0.74], pFDR < 0.001).

Comparison of Normative Reference and Clinical Relevance with T2-WMHyperV across HCs and Brain Disorders Based on the available T2-WMHyperV (n=2,276 for HCs, and n=2,939 for brain disorders), we first analyzed the correlations between absolute raw T1-WMHyoV and T2-WMHyperV by univariate Pearson correlation across HC and disease groups.
Then we fitted the normative reference of T2-WMHyperV with the same method as described in the T1-WMHypoV normative reference construction.
